I’ve had a mixed relationship with Dragons Dogma. I initially had a lot of problems with the first few hours and called it quits. I restarted a few weeks later, and then thought the game was kind of clunky but fun enough to continue. Following this, I had a 40ish hour period where I thought Dragons Dogma was a really under-appreciated experience and that it was one of the better games I’ve played recently. As I came closer to the end, I came to the conclusion that Dragons Dogma is a heavily mediocre game with a lot of half-baked ideas that come together in a strange package.

DD:DA gives you a surprising amount of freedom with how you play. There are a variety of classes with different playstyles, and you are encouraged to switch around often. You also get to customize a pawn, which is an AI companion, and hire two others from other players. Pawns have personalities and can be wildly different from each other. You're able to hire pawns that have quest knowledge to help guide you, or pay more for stronger pawns who steamroll through enemies. There are a huge number of quests, and a huge world to explore. The combat has a satisfying punch to it, and fighting certain beasts is crazy fun because you can do crazy things like climb up them, hack off tusks, break arms, and more. 

Regarding the variety in monsters, you’ll quickly realize that there are not very many things you actually fight in this game. Not too many varieties exist and it’s kind of disappointing that there aren’t a larger variety of enemies to face. Cyclops and griffins are fun to fight, but once you’ve killed your 30th cyclops it’s just not that engaging anymore.

The world is sparsely populated and a good 40% of your playtime will be jogging from one side of the map to the other. The quest design is kind of crappy in that you won't have too many clusters of quests to do at once... you'll run for fifteen minutes to talk to someone for a minute. You then either have the joy of running all the way back, or hopefully having a consumable item to use. The fast travel teleporting is janky, and although you can set your own waypoints, it doesn't fix how grueling it can be to set them up. I've had tons of odd quest bugs as well, like freezing NPCs. The game has a distinct layer of Capcom jank all over it.

The pawn system is the coolest part of this game. You get to customize an AI companion and they learn the game along with you. You can rent other players pawns and bring them along, and they bring knowledge from their worlds. Pawns will also learn knowledge from you and bring them back to their masters. The system has a learning curve, but it is all pretty simple once you get the hang of it. Pawns are a really fun part of the game, however they annoyingly seem to never shut up, so you’ll constantly have between one and three companions constantly babbling about almost nothing. Occasionally a pawn will drop a good hint on how to defeat a monster or a shortcut to take in a quest, but most of the time they seem to just ramble about things they’re observing.

To add to all of this, you'll randomly get cut off from tons of quests or storylines just because you accidentally did a thing, and a mechanic that is never explained to you plays a massive role in the ending. I ended up having a wiki open all the time to hopefully not miss out on something, and constantly alt-tabbing to use a wiki gets annoying. Even then, I kept finding out I had just locked myself out of the best way to get discounts in the game or some really useful equipment. Even though these things would only be fleetingly useful and most of the quests you get locked out of aren't very engaging anyway, it sucks to talk to someone and then suddenly fail ten quests for no discernable reason.

I've really enjoyed playing this game at times, but sometimes the design decisions frustrate the hell out of me. Some people really love the endgame, but I’ve found it to be an obnoxious grind and it feels like I am punished for not following a min-max guide to beat the game, as I’ve missed a ton of quests and my characters stats aren’t ideal. I could run the two endgame dungeons over and over and over again hoping for rare (2% - 8%) drops from certain chests in order to gear up to do the dungeons even faster and maybe kill the endgame bosses which provide you better gear to kill themselves with… or I could just finish the game and call it good.

Notably, there is a NG+ mode, so if you find that you actually really love this game (which I know some do), you can keep the adventure rolling.

If I could, I'd give this a middle rating. I'd kind of recommend it, but some things really suck about it and might prevent some people from enjoying it. I dunno. Sure, I'll give it a thumbs up. I have had some good times with it… but a whole lot of bad ones, too.

I played this game on Xbox360 when it was first released back in 2012. I thought it was a pretty awesome game but I never got that far into it because I found it very differcult and it had a very minimal and frustrating fast-travel system. But this game had a very intriguing open-world and combat system. So when I heard that it was being released on PC earlier this year I got really excited and pre-ordered it and jumped straight into it on release-day.
It was everything I had remembered plus more. The lack of fast-travel had been fixed and a great new system of travel had been implemented. The player can aquire an item called "Portcrystals" that they can then place anywhere in the over-world and teleport to them as many times as they want. They can also be picked up and put down somewhere else. I really enjoyed this freedom to customise where I could instantly teleport to, put it didn't hinder my incentive to explore.

I think this game probably has some of the best-looking combat in a video-game I've ever come across. The magic looks beautiful, the monsters you fight are huge and epic. It's a party-based game so you make up 1/4 of your team. The AI is extremely intelligent, and I found it quite refreshing to not have to do ALL the work in a combat situation. 

Your allies (referred to as "Pawns" in-game) are always activiely learning about quests as you do them and monsters as you fight them. This creates very dynamic gameplay. And I would always find myself being impressed with my parties capabilities during a fight or quest, whether it be casting a healing-spell or using their sheild to spring-board my assassin up onto the shoulders of an enemy cyclopes or gathering herbs or mining ore and so-on...

This game offers the usual aspects of a good RPG: gathering / crafting, exploration, NPC relationships, dialogue choices, class ranks and a character level range from 1-200.

The story is absolutely fantastic and I was blown-away at how everything all added up at the end of my first playthrough. This game is based around the player completing subsequent playthroughs to get through some of the end-game content. And what's really impressive is that it actually manages to tie it all in with it's lore and story. 
On my first playthrough, I thought some of the events that happened as part of the story were a bit weird and ambiguous, but as soon as I finished my first playthrough it all made sense and everything had it's purpose.

The Steam version of Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen includes the expansion which is basically a differcult mega-dungeon aimed at players who are progressing through the late-game. It has a very Dark Souls feel to it.

Overall, I would give this game a [b] 9 / 10 [/b]
The graphics are still beautiful and the combat is some of the most impressive and dynamic and epic I've come across in a video-game. I have some great memories of playing this game and I would recommend it to any RPG fan or Skyrim fan looking for something a bit more hardcore but found Dark Souls too differcult :P

I've been playing this game elsewhere and am approaching 200 hours. What spurred me into trying this game again was a playthrough of Elden Ring. 

I'm going to talk about Elden Ring a bit, sorry. Skip to "AIGHT NOW IT BIG BOY HOURS" to skip past Elden Ring rant.

Elden Ring is a big game. It's very big. It's also a difficult game for the unprepared, or, most importantly, those wishing to play in a closed ecosystem. By this I mean, playing Elden Ring without relying on the internet for anything.
Not looking up where to go, not looking up the best builds, et cetera et cetera. Talking to friends and sharing tips between one another is fine, but no Google or forums or wikis. It was fun for a bit but around hour 50 I realized I was miserable, and by hour 80 I was fed up. 

I knew where to go for the main story, that's not really a problem if you listen to dialogue, what was a problem is that I was woefully underpowered and trying to follow any side questline was an exercise in futility. 

I needed to look stuff up to figure out what was wrong with my build, and to figure out where did x NPC go after suddenly disappearing.
You shouldn't have to do that. 
I did it because I really did need to. I found all the OP stuff I'd missed, and of course I saw the extent of the exploits and cheese that Elden Ring's spaghetti code has to offer for those inclined for an easier experience. The mystery was gone, the curtain was pulled back and it felt like that was what the developers intended.

I genuinely believe that Elden Ring was made to be so overwhelming and ridiculously bloated that you NEED to rely on the internet. You NEED to go to Youtube and engage with content creators, you NEED to go to forums. You NEED to go online and TALK ABOUT ELDEN RING.
You've gotta go talk about this game because it's so big and crazy and hard and WoOOOaAAahhhHHh!

I'm sure there are people that want a game like that. A game that is incredibly obtuse and vague that will take a lot of time to figure out. I understand that, but I don't think Elden Ring handled it well. It's too obtuse, and too big to allow itself to be that obtuse. La Mulana, an infamously cryptic game, handled this far better and it's an older game made by just one guy I believe. 

An example of Elden Ring being too obscure for its own good: I had a "journal" for La Mulana, to help keep track of everything and solve puzzles. I remember having wonderful epiphanies from pouring over my notes, as if the game wanted me to do this. It wanted me to solve its mysteries. The game would often hand out clues like numbered dots that lined up in sequence upon reviewing them, it was remarkable.
I also had a "journal" for Elden Ring. I took notes and tried to keep track of everything. The game rarely handed out clues, and when it did, they were inconsequential, or simply stating the obvious. The dots weren't numbered and they didn't connect in any way. The game clearly did not want me to solve the many mysteries it was presenting. Rather, I felt that the game wanted me to treat Google like a how-to manual.

It wasn't until very recently, maybe hour 160 or 170 in my Dragon's Dogma playthrough that I decided to google something I didn't know. Why? Because I was never desperate for answers before that. The game isn't necessarily cryptic like La Mulana, but it does have mysteries and it does have a layer of obtuseness that can tickle the brain. The curtain stays firmly in place in Dragon's Dogma and the developers definitely don't want you to pull it back, they want to be your dungeon master in this world and take you on a journey! An epic quest!

Elden Ring doesn't have a dungeon master, it feels like a literal dungeon with guards that poke and prod at the player and dare them to do anything other than call out their window for help, which is, ironically, completely OK in that dungeon.

This is a small world that is easily digestible. It wants you to take your time and explore. It wants you to grow and learn within this space and through repeated playthroughs. There are easily missed things (the game has like 6 point-of-no-returns, it's a bit silly and one of the only things that warrant a google search) but it's not frustrating to miss these, because new game+ is just around the corner whenever you want it to be, given the story's brief length once you know where to go. 
It's a world of danger and just [i] enough [/i] mystery. You probably won't need to keep a "journal" for Dragon's Dogma, but you also won't feel it necessary to rely on Google just to beat the game.

[h1][i][b]Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen[/b][/i][/h1]

[h1]Recommended purchase point: [b]FULL PRICE[/b][/h1]

If The Witcher 3 didn't exist, I'd call this my favourite RPG of the 2010s. Don't get me wrong - there are a few things Dragon's Dogma does that other games do better, but... it just has this invisible 'X factor'. Perhaps it would be better described as a kind of warmth: it's plain to see that genuine love and passion went into the creation of this game, and that is something that makes a game more than the sum of its parts. 

[h1]STORY[/h1] [b][i]What a large tree....[/i][/b]

The game's story seems initially like generic fantasy fare - slay the dragon that attacked your village - but soon develops into something genuinely interesting and borderline philosophical. Connected to this is the pawn hiring system, a unique and enjoyable way to interact with your fellow players (and make a healthy profit in the process). When you begin the game you create two characters: your player character and your pawn, a permanent AI partner who can learn behaviours and even personality quirks from the example you set ingame. 

[h1]PAWNS[/h1] [b][i]'Tis even larger up close![/i][/b]

After a certain point in the story you gain the ability to visit the Rift, where the pawns of every other online player are available for you to hire and round out your party (to a maximum of 4 members). Your created pawn will also go up for hire in the Rift, and will periodically bring back payments from other players who may have hired them. 

Capcom have created a fantastic hiring system, giving you access to nearly infinite party members with a wealth of personality created by your fellow players and letting you feel connected to the community at large even in a singleplayer game like this. The pawns themselves possess a fantastically Ye-Olde-English-as-written-by-a-Japanese-writer dialect, which sounds annoying on paper but actually gives them a huge amount of charm in practice.

[h1]COMBAT[/h1] [b][i]The beast fears fire![/i][/b]

Dragon's Dogma's combat system is probably the most consistently fun of any action RPG out there. Fighters and Striders use nimble attacks (some of them lifted directly from Devil May Cry) and freedom of mobility to climb all over large monsters in search of the optimum place to deal damage. Rangers deal damage from afar with a longbow that feels absurdly powerful and impactful, unlike the archery option in many other RPGs. Mages and sorcerers unleash some of the most devastating magic spells seen in any RPG. That isn't even getting into the hybrid classes. They're all great.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]

This is the third time I have bought this game and I would frankly happily do it again to drill it into Capcom's head that [i]I want another one.[/i]

Dragon's Dogma is a unique, brilliant yet flawed underrated gem.

I bought the game on it's PC release and didn't really get into it. I was fresh out of Dark Souls 1 and 2, and 3 was about to release. The game had it's charm, but looked kinda dated and lacked complexity in both story and gameplay compared to the Souls series I was infused in. I played a couple hours and forgot about it.

After a year of DS3, Rocket League and getting back into Skyrim among other things, I looked for new games to play. I was craving something new to lose myself into like I did with the Souls series. I noticed Dragon's Dogma being mentioned by a small fraction of Souls enthusiasts, which puzzled me as I personally didn't get the vibe from it. For lack of better options though, I decided to give it another try.

Dragon's Dogma isn't Dark Souls, or Skyrim, or Shadow of the Collossus, or Final Fantasy or any other RPG. Dragon's Dogma is unique in that it attempts to combine complex existing features in a coherent, living world and adds innovations on top. Such an ambitious attempt comes with flaws, but also with unexpected brilliance.

Dragon's Dogma is open world, in that you have a vast world to explore. While most of the game's content resides in the main storyline, the game does allow you to freely roam the world at any point, and has many side quests.

The main storyline may appear pretty weak and generic at first. I know it did for me. Not until the very end of my first playthrough did I realize the true scale of it. I really recommend playing this game with an open mind, as it is much deeper than it originally seems. And yes, if you get into it, you -will- want to do a second playthrough. ;)

DD is an Action-RPG. Combat is real time and occurs as you run into enemies. You have a wide variety of classic classes to chose from, and can switch vocations indefinitely. Each vocation's skill trees unlock as you level them, and reach unsuspected levels of complexity, resulting in an extremely varied gaming experience depending on which class you play.

Combat is one of the strongest points of the game. It manages to be both fast paced and tactical. And epic! Yes a lot of it will be mowing down goblins and thieves, but run into one of the bigger monsters and that's where the real fun begins. The way to bring down these will be up to you, but they all have their weaknesses and depending on your class you'll have a different role in that. Hack at it's feet to weaken it's defense, or cling to it's leg to unbalance it, while your archer companion snipes at it's one eye and the mage rains bolts upon it. Or climb all the way to it's head to remove it's giant helmet and stun it while the warrior concentrate all of his strength in his massive two-handed sword to deliver the killing blow. Add the epic orchestral choir driven soundtrack in the background, and there you have it: the game absolutely succeeds in giving you this grand feeling of fighting giant monsters as a team while giving you total freedom and keeping it fast-paced, and this is quite an achievement in my opinion.

Speaking of team, let's talk of pawns. Dragon's Dogma is a single player game. With a twist. On character creation, you'll be able to create a secondary non playable character: your "pawn". Ingame, you'll gain access to special stones, which allows you to recruit 2 other pawns on top of your main one. These other pawns were created by other players and you can hire them for free if they are your own level or below, or use a special currency for higher level ones. Your own pawn will be available for rent to other players as well.

This may seem trivial at first, but there's more to it. As you progress through the game, explore the map, complete quests and fight enemies, your pawn will gradually learn about all these things. He will learn to not run head first into this particular foe, but to target specific parts. He will also learn when he travels with other players, and may surprise you by showing you the path to a hidden cave you didn't notice, or giving you hints on a quest you didn't complete yet. All of these he will know because he experienced it while being rented by someone else. He will also learn from your actions and behavior, and gain certain orientations from it. You'll have the possibility to shape and reorient these by talking to him in certain locations. This gives whole new aspects to the game, as how your pawn shapes will directly alter his fighting performances, and the rental system expand the illusion of the world's existence beyond your own experience. Your pawn will also collect a particular currency while being rented which becomes really useful in later parts of the game, which gives more incentive to perfect him. Should be noted that there's still a quite active community of very friendly pawn trading players if you would so wish to give into that kind of online interactions. By no means a necessity though.

So there you have it. A classic looking single player open world action RPG with hints of multiplayer, a story with a twist, super epic battles and a LOT of content.

Beat the main game ? If you're like me you'll feel compelled to go ng+. The game strongly encourages you to do so anyway. Feeling overpowered ? Why not head to Bitterblack Isle, the DLC area of the game ? The Dark Souls vibe is strong with that one, and it'll kick your ass even if your second playthrough of the main game felt like a breeze. And yes, there's a hard mode if you want extra challenge. Want more Dragon action ? The Ur-Dragon becomes available on ng+. You'll be able to take the offline version on your own afer a while, but the online one takes days of players from the entire world fighting it to take down, and you can claim your part of the loot when it finally does. There's lots to do, but if you end up falling in love with the game like I and others did, you'll be left wishing the game was more successful and got more DLCs, and join the club of people praying it finally gets the sequel it deserves.

The game has it's flaws, naturally. You forgive them after a while when you measure how ambitious it was. The pawn system can be frustrating at times, as well as the questing one. The game also introduces an "affinity" system, with which you naturally build gradual relationship bonds with any NPC you interact with in the world, which is both interesting and flawed as well. The main story goes through confusing and/or incoherent and sometimes plain uninteresting moments, but redeems itself in the end. The main gaming events themselves will sometimes get boring with a lot of back and forth, only to surprise you again with a sudden unexpected epic confrontation ... It's a game that by it's overambitious nature would have necessitated much more polishing and optimization, but still managed to achieve a surprisingly great amount of it's goals.

All in all, yes: flawed in many ways ... yet unique, brilliant and epic. I really, really recommend you give it a real try if you're a RPG enthusiast.

Oh and the soundtrack is a-ma-zing.

After over 100 hours on the original console version and nearly another 100 on PC, the conclusion I've come to on Dragon's Dogma is that it is not the greatest RPG of all time - but it is the tech demo for it.

Often touted as the love child of Dark Souls, Monster Hunter, and Shadow of the Colossus, the combat of Dragon's Dogma is easily its greatest strength, and more than makes up for some of the more glaring issues that the game possesses. Scaling a raging cyclops and stabbing it in the eye is just as fun the 50th time as it is the first time you do it. This combat system is greatly benefited by the nine different classes to choose from, with the standard combat triangle of fighter, rogue, and mage, as well as advanced, specialized variants of those, and even hybrid vocations. With so many skills and weapon archetypes to choose from, there's definitely something for everyone in this game. The pawn system is another unique and versatile mechanic that adds to excellent foundation that the combat system presents, allowing for meticulous tweaking of party composition for almost any environment. The Everfall and Bitterblack Isle are where the combat truly shines, allowing for short downtime between fights as you travel through their various chambers encountering the more fun and engaging enemies in the game.

The only two issues I have with the combat system as is would be the often ridiculous stat scaling and the consumable item mechanics. With an effectively unrestricted world to explore right from the get go, there are numerous areas that basically serve the purpose of being "noob traps", slaughtering unsuspecting new players who wander off the initial path the game expects of them. Enemies like chimeras, drakes, and even simple bandits can decimate low-level parties in an instant, with very little way of determining their strength beyond the "smack it and see what happens" approach. While enemy-specific weaknesses go beyond simple elemental variants to include targeting specific body parts is a fantastic mechanic, it is greatly hampered by how the game handles gear and stat scaling. Eventually as you progress, you will come to a point where you tear through common enemies like fodder, turning normal-sized enemies into an annoyance rather than a threat. This is exacerbated by instantaneous effects of potions and other consumables, which makes combat lose its sense of intensity and urgency once you are well stocked. And that doesn't even factor in wakestones, which can virtually remove any consequence from death if desired. Of course, this can be mitigated by limiting yourself to a set amount of potions, but I feel like a different healing system would have greatly benefited this game.

The last thing I'll mention is the story, which is generally one of the more negatively viewed aspects of the game. The general gist is that you are the "Arisen", someone who controls the Pawn Legion (pseudo-humans with no free will) on your quest to kill a dragon that stole your heart (literally). While I found the climax with the dragon and everything that follows until completion of the story to be very enjoyable and even thought-provoking, everything leading up to the dragon showdown feels like nothing more than a vessel to get you to that point with very little thought put into its pacing, coordination or design in general. Bland, one-dimensional characters, uninspired fetch/kill quests, and a railroaded love-interest with actual worst girl The Dutchess leave a sour taste in my mouth, even after the ending segments of the story manage to redeem the overall narrative. Whether the product of rushed production, discombobulated ideas, or simply being lost in translation, there's a very good reason many people recommend rushing to the post-dragon content as quickly as possible.

There are many more highly promising aspects of this game that I feel didn't get enough love during development, such as the map, romance system, inventory management, and more, but this review is already long enough. So instead:

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Despite its many issues, Dragon's Dogma is a criminally underrated and overlooked game that every RPG fan should try. Given enough time and love during development to build upon the solid foundation it has provided, its sequel (please Itsuno) could easily become my favorite game of all time.

[h1]PROS[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Greatest combat in an action RPG to date
    [*]Varied class vocations
    [*]Pawn system
    [*]Exciting enemies
    [*]Enemy-specific learning curve (elements, weak points, etc.)
    [*]Highly replayable endgame
    [*]Locations with radiant enemy spawns
    [*]Beautiful soundtrack
    [*]Interesting climax/resolution to the story
    [*]Interesting romance system
[/list]

[h1]CONS[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Poor stat scaling and healing mechanics
    [*]Story, characters, and quests need work
    [*]Deceptively sized, sparsely populated map
    [*]Inventory management becomes tedious
[/list]

[h1]An ARPG good enough to make you look past its dull and lifeless setting [/h1]

Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen is the recently released PC version of Capcom’s third person ARPG which was originally released in 2012. You live in a small fishing village called Cassardis in a province called Gransys. Gransys is in a world filled with mythical creatures ranging from small goblins to huge chimeras but that makes the events of the game’s first day no less shocking to those who inhabit this fictional world. A dragon is summoned by dark and mysterious forces and his first target is Cassardis. Watching most of the people you know die horribly at the hands of the dragon spurs you into action, armed with nothing but a sword you give the dragon all you’ve got. The dragon bats you away as if you are nothing more than a fly but instead of killing you, the dragon steals your heart, binding your life to that of the dragon and you become the Arisen. The Arisen is believed to be the only person in the world capable of defeating the dragon and so you become an incredibly important person in Gransys.

As with all games, the first thing you’ll notice about DD: DA is how it looks. Being a game that originally released around four years ago, the graphics aren’t exactly cutting edge and some of the textures aren’t what you’d call easy on the eye but there is a real improvement over the original game and it does look pretty good. One of the main problems with the original release of the game was its poor performance but thankfully that’s all been fixed now. Even with a PC in the middle of minimum and recommended (with a pretty weak GPU) I’m able to run the game pretty much maxed out with a stable 30FPS. The UI and menus are all pretty good though you can tell they were made for console rather than PC, I played with a controller so I didn’t have any issues but playing with M&KB may be a bit of a pain at times.

Moving on to gameplay, DD: DA is what you’d expect from a third person ARPG. The game offers you a choice of six basic vocations (classes) and three hybrid vocations (a combination of two basic ones). The basic vocations are all what you’d expect, you’ve got two fighter classes, two ranged/dagger classes and two magic-based classes. Each vocation comes with specific equipment (though most equipment can be used by similar vocations, not just one), skills (active and passive) and of course a unique playstyle. Active skills consist of weapon-specific special attacks such as a skill which lets you fire six arrows at once for the ranged classes and spells for the magic-based classes. The passive skills are again unique to each vocation and offer you certain bonuses such as more health at night time or take less damage when your weapons are sheathed. 

DD: DA’s unique selling point is its pawn system. You have one main pawn and two other pawns when you’re playing the game. Your main pawn is effectively a second character but one that is not controller by the player, meaning you decide what they look like, wear, use as weapons etc. but you don’t actually control them. Your main pawn can be any one of the six basic vocations and it’s often wise to switch between them once you’ve reached the max vocation level so you can get useful skills from other vocations. The other two pawns are other people’s main pawns and you have no control over them. There’s a place in the game called The Rift, accessed using Rift Stones, and you can go there to search for and enlist two pawns. As you go through the game, your main pawn will receive knowledge on enemies, missions and locations after you’ve encountered said things and they will then relay helpful information about these things to any other players who decide to enlist your pawns. Once you’re done using a pawn you ‘send it back’ with a gift for its creator as well as a basic review of its appearance and effectiveness. It’s important to have a good mix of pawns of different vocations so you’ll need to play around with your set up to get it just right.

Being an ARPG, there’s a hell of a lot of fighting in DD: DA. Unfortunately, fighting regular mobs is pretty tedious as they don’t pose much challenge at all and they feel like they’ve just been placed into what is already a bland game world. Thankfully DD: DA’s boss fights more than make up for the disappointing mobs. Most of the bosses are absolutely huge, have loads of health and deal incredible amounts of damage. What makes boss fights so much fun is that you can climb on large enemies, allowing you to attack them up close and personal as well as allowing you to more easily exploit their weaknesses. Boss fights also award you with huge EXP rewards as well as a fair bit of loot, usually in the form of rare crafting materials. 

I’ll briefly return to the issue of the bland game world, one of two major issues with the game. Gransys simply doesn’t feel like a real place. The two cities in the game have small populations and feel pretty empty when you’re wandering around them but outside the cities the problem is even worse. You can sometimes go a couple of minutes without seeing anyone and since the game involves a lot of long and tedious travelling (thanks to the lack of a proper fast travel system, my other major issue with the game) the world feels all the more empty. While you can set up a fast travel system later on in the game using a limited number of rare items, early on in the game you have to walk across what is a rather large map with the occasional sprints in between waiting for your stamina bar to slowly recharge.

Once you’re done with the base game you can move on to post-game, Dark Arisen and then unlimited New Game plus runs as well as a hard mode and speedrun mode. Post-game offers more challenging enemies and loot while Dark Arisen is the game’s only DLC and again offers more challenging enemies, particularly more challenging boss fights. After completing all that and going through the final mission of post-game you’re given the option to start the game again but with the same character, skills and equipment which can then be done every time you beat the game, offering endless replayability though you’ll probably be done with the game after your second run.

[h1]Verdict [/h1]

[b]Worth Purchasing. [/b]

Despite taking place in a bland world, DD: DA’s fantastic pawn system and boss fights make this an ARPG that’s well worth playing. DD: DA may not be as tough as some games but it does provide enough of a challenge to make completing it and even just beating some of the harder bosses incredibly satisfying. If you like a good third person ARPG, do yourself a favour and pick this one up.

Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen
(WARNING: LONG BUT INSIGHTFUL REVIEW AHEAD)

Recommended purchase point: On Sale (~$10)

Don't let my hours fool you, I have a little over 200 hours back on the old Xbox 360 when I first started this game.  I would definitely say that this is one of my favorite RPG games that I've ever played.  It's caters almost entirely to the player and their specific playstyles, and gives them the freedom tackle quests and foes in a multitude of ways.  It's aged just a bit since its initial release since 2012 (Dark Arisen is the DLC to this game released in 2016), and has some things it does well and some things that are implemented poorly, but I will get into all of those below.

STORY - 7/10

It's kind of a basic fantasy RPG plot, where big mean dragon attacks your village, and you go off to destroy it in hopes to save your country.  But where the plot ends is where the story begins in my honest opinion.  I won't go into explicit detail on where or when in order to save you the chance of experiencing it yourself, but I will hint that things get pretty crazy towards the endgame, making it a very thought provoking and questionable conclusion.

Dark Arisen is the DLC expansion where you arrive on a mysterious and monster ridden island and delve into its depths in order to solve a mysterious and dark mystery.  Easily my favorite part of the game for some more lore-related knowledge, a brutal dungeon to delve into, and amazing loot to reward the challenge. (Personally a 10/10 IMO).

A word of advice is that some choices in the late game can lead to different endings, and a lot of the time you can restart from a point just before you make that decision, so don't be afraid to experiment a little!  And take every quest that's offered to you! 

GRAPHICS - 8/10

It's nothing too fancy, but if you have the power on your computer, crank up some of your settings in order to enjoy a vibrant and beautiful game.  There's a lot going on during combat as well so you're bound to enjoy cranking up your effects setting in order to enjoy all of the pretty magic effects going on.

SOUND/MUSIC - 8/10

The sound in this game is pretty amazing given its age.  Trees whistle in the wind as you walk through forests, gravel crunches at your feet as you sneak around, flesh rips and tears as you slice through your enemies, it’s a truly satisfying experience for your ears.

I will admit that some overworld music can be a little repetitive during your playthrough, but once you start combat with giant monsters, you get some crazy ass and intense music playing while you fight.  Easily one of my favorite parts of the game, but again, the overworld music can be a little obnoxious at times.

GAMEPLAY - 7/10

I'm going to give you a quick TL;DR on this aspect so I don't spoil much of anything.  In addition to creating your own character, you have the option to create a second, permanent party member who will accompany you along your journey.  You have full customization over this character (class, appearance, armor, skills, etc.) and it can be rented and used by other characters throughout their journey.  Your second character (or Pawn as the game calls it) is an infant of sorts and needs to learn based on experiences through your journey and the journeys of those who've rented them.  The knowledge they obtain helps them fight better against specific foes or help guide you through areas that they are aware of.  The biggest thing is that they mimic and follow actions based on what you do in combat (i.e. if you target smaller threats over bigger ones, then your Pawn will do the same.  Or if you choose to loot items over fighting enemies when in battle, your Pawn will follow your lead).  

It's a neat concept on paper, but I won't lie when I say that the A.I. can be incredibly idiotic in some cases.  Sometimes these actions (or Inclinations as the game puts it) are mostly undesirable (like having a mage climb and attack bigger enemies instead of casting spells from a distance).  They can be overwritten through a method better explained on the Wiki, but it can be annoying to deal with at times.

Perhaps my biggest gripe I have with the Pawn system is that they refuse to stop talking no matter what.  I'm not joking when I say they can blabber on for the entire day about the area that they're in or give advice on the most blatantly obvious things around you.  The odds that they say something even remotely useful are very slim, so be prepared for questing with individuals who think and act like children on a regular basis.  (Again, my opinion, as some players seem to enjoy the Pawn's discussions).

The game is incredibly challenging on its own, forcing you to adapt your tactics or gear to best accommodate a variety of threats that you might encounter.  Hard Mode is recommended if you really crave a challenge, but I warn you it becomes Dark Souls difficult at that point (especially on the Dark Arisen expansion).  Best to start with Normal Mode if you are a first-time player.

COMBAT - 10/10 (HIGHLY RECOMMEND PLAYING WITH A CONTROLLER)

I have to be perfectly honest here, Capcom did an amazing job when it came to implementing combat in this game.  It's fluid and fresh, while being simple and easy to learn at the same time.  Given the amount of options you have in this game in terms of skills, passive abilities, weapons, and armor, you can easily equip your character to fit your playstyle almost entirely.

Vocations are the game's term for classes in Dragon's Dogma, and each class has their own unique set of skills, armor types, and weapons that they can utilize.  A cool thing to note is that some vocations share skills with each other, so if you unlock a sword skill on one vocation, you can carry over to another vocation if they use the sword as well.  Even cooler are passive abilities, which can be used by all vocations and can be mixed and matched for great effects on your character and/or Pawn.  

I'm going to go a little more in depth on classes and their architypes right now, so brace yourself here:

First you have Basic, or Starting Vocations, which consist of the Fighter, the Strider, and the Mage.  You can then upgrade to Advanced Vocations like the Warrior, Ranger, or Sorcerer.  Finally, you have Hybrid Vocations which combine two basic vocations together into one crazy unique class, something that I haven't seen in a lot of RPG's at all.  These consist of the Mystic Knight (Fighter x Mage), Assassin (Strider x Fighter), and Magick Archer (Mage x Strider).  All of these vocations boast incredible skills, from summoning a giant meteor storm, to brutally gouging a sword into giant enemies, to rapid firing ten arrows at once.  The effects and sheer power behind these skills is incredibly satisfying and rewarding, which is something that keeps me grounded in big RPGs like this. And the absolute best part is that you can switch classes whenever you want with no real drawbacks (If you're really worried about character growth you can min/max stats by sticking to a class and switching around other classes at certain points when you level up, but I recommend playing how you want for your first time through).

Fights both big and small are amazing and rewarding experiences.  Again, I promise not to spoil anything, but trust me when I say your first encounters with new monsters (especially big ones) will always be memorable.

CONCLUSION - 9/10
.
An incredible, and satisfying buy that can easily be worth your time.  If you like RPGs, Fantasy, Fast Paced Combat, or Open Worlds, then this is the game for you

Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen is an action role playing game, developed by Capcom. The original game was released on PS3 and Xbox 360 in 2013, before the game was finally ported to PC in January 2016. 

The game starts with your character being super overpowered, with really rare equipment and dealing tons of damage, giving you a sneak peak into the type of end game content you have to come. But yes, you do get nerfed back down to the regular level 1 RPG character, in your rags and sticks for swords. You are able to choose between a number of different classes, or vocations as they are called in DD. On top of being in control of your character, you will also gain a party of up to three more “pawns”, these too take on specific roles in the group, such as tanks, damage and healers. I found this to be a really nice addition to the game as I wasn’t expecting such mechanics from an RPG game like this. The party controls and management system is basic at best, but the AI is fairly in tune with what they should be doing, and the two basic controls, attack and follow, are both really responsive as well. 

The combat system in DD against the smaller style of enemies is very generic hack and slash, there is no real special combos or special abilities to come across, The warrior class is probably the most basic class to play, but is probably the one I would recommend for your first play through.  Where DD’s combat system really comes into its own, is when you get to scale larger enemies, such as giants, and cyclops.  This allows you to climb onto enemies backs and swing at them to deal more damage. This is a feature that I haven’t really seen incorporated into combat systems in recent memory, the last time I remember coming across it is in Shadow of the Colossus.   

You can definitely tell this game was ported from the consoles as the graphics are average at best. The game is pretty poorly optimized as even though the graphics didn’t look brilliant, I wasn’t able to get the full 4k effect. The character models look pretty good once you get some more interesting looking armour and weapons to equip. Animation across the game is of a high standard though, with the regular combat hack and slash animations looking very cool when you can couple a few attacks together. You can get some really nice visual effects through the draw distance of the PC version of the game being superior, with some really nice looking environments when you are out in the open world.  This is a game which is completely voice acted, all to a really high standard as well. 

DD is a pretty hard game, even on the lower difficulty throughs, you will have challenges. You can really run into high level enemies without realizing it’s too late and your attacks do no damage at all. You have to make use of the game’s block system and your excessively large jump range too in order to dodge attacks and swipes. The use of the pawn system really aids the inexperienced players though, as they scale with your level too.

Whilst DD has a really large open world for you to explore, it is really tedious to travel to and from places. The lack of any staple fast travel system without having to use consumables is a real pain. There was nothing more demoralizing than getting a quest, then seeing it was at the completely opposite side of the map, only to get there, and they tell you to go straight back. This problem at times almost made me not want to continue. There is a fast travel system, but it is not easily accessible and you require items which are not very common to find in the game too. 

Completing the game took me twenty hours. I will admit, I didn’t complete as many side quests as I would normally, and this was purely down to the giant map, and no fast travel system. The side quest system is also pretty in-depth too; because if you go too far in the main story line, you are unable to complete some side quests, which means if you want to go for the complentionists approach to this game, you best get that Wiki bookmarked to make sure you don’t miss out on anything! I would say there is an element of replay ability, not only does the game have a New game+ mode, but also has a speed run mode which is nice to see. You could also get another play through out of playing as a different class to change up the variety a bit. 

Technically, the game is sound. I didn’t have any crashes or bugs. The graphic side of the game is poorly optimized as my rig should be able to cope with his game on ultra-settings but sadly it got some chugging and frame drops on the higher graphical options. You can tell the game is a console port as the menus are clearly made for consoles, and do not incorporate the use of keyboard and mouse very easily. That being said, I did play the game completely with a keyboard and mouse but the game could quite easily be played using a controller. 

In summary, Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen is a really good action RPG game. The only negatives I found are the poorer graphics, and the annoying fast travel system. If these aren’t problems which will grind on you, then DD is a stellar game. The combat system is really interesting, along with an intriguing story line. If you manage to complete all of the side quests on offer, you could easily get 30 or so hours out of this game, plus any further runs you do in the other game modes. The game is really nicely priced at £23,99. I am going with a highly recommendation of this game

Hmm. Where to start? I guess I'll be blunt and say this one of my favorite Capcom games/favorite RPGs of all time. The game feels like a combination of Monster Hunter and Devil May Cry, albeit amplifying and capitalizing on the former's missed potential. The gameplay is smooth and has a touch of DMC-inspired action to it, though not as over-the-top. The Pawn system is an interesting concept and appeals to the side of me that likes watching the AI do the dirty work for me. There are times though when the AI does come up short, but even still it is very competent. 

The Monster Hunter aspect of combat is more-or-less fully realized in letting you actually climb on monsters in real-time while they try to shake you off, rather than a pseudo-minigame like in 4U. It's very satisfying to work together with your Pawns and watch them unleash both spell and steel in combination with your own attacks to barrage an enemy into defeat. The game also has pretty nice pacing when it comes to making each encounter more strenous and epic, leading all the way up to one of the best boss/dragon fights I've ever seen in a game. Enemies like the Gryphon actually feel like they're doing everything in their ability to take you down. Rather than have the AI purposely handicap itself by frequently staying on the ground, enemies that can fly will do so to make sure you have a hard time conquering them (which is where the Pawn/AI system works to compliment your tactics). Wrangling a large creature also feels more like a risk/reward tactic rather than a push "A" to win scenario. An enemy will do their best to shake you off, robbing you of stamina, and possibly your life if they fling you off the edge of a large drop.

The implementation and execution of the Pawn system is, for the most part, well done. Players can "share" Pawns with other players around the world. While with them, or with you they will level and can learn about new tactics for enemies or how to fulfill quests. When they are returned to their original owner, they will keep this knowledge to better serve you.


The negatives to the game come in the form of the camera sometimes being erratic when mounting a creature, or being under the feet of a large enemy. I would have liked some alpha transparency use for when the camera collides with models in a fight. Though considering how easily the fighting system lets you pull out of a bad situation, such an issue will rarely be the cause of death. Pawns can also seem a bit too timid at times, and will refuse to capitalize on chances to heavily punish an enemy. Traveling may also grind on players until they start knowing when and where to place down port crystals. It seems this issue was partially mitigated with the addition of an "Eternal Ferrystone" with infinite uses, though you will at some points have to plan out long journeys on foot. If you're expecting a heavy emphasis on RPG choice elements like in a Bioware game, you'll be left wanting here. There are some sections of the game that are dependant on how you approach a situation, but most are black and white choices.

As a port, the game is well-optimized and further remedies any camera problems by allowing one to change the FOV. There are 4k textures as well for more powerful setups, though don't expect the game to look amazing even with them on.

Overall, if you're looking for an Open-World, RPG with a intuitive combat system/AI creation and some epic fights I'd highly recommend Dragon's Dogma.

In May of 2012, a much underappreciated generational masterpiece was released, Dragon's Dogma.  Unfortunately it was released six months after Skyrim, and was completely drowned out by the hype for that game following its release.  A year later, the expansion Dark Arisen launched adding the much beloved Bitter Black Isle.  Three years after that, it would finally come to Steam.  And now nine years later I'm finally giving it a review.  My first review for any game bought on Steam, despite owning dozens of them.  I played Dragon's Dogma Dark Arisen extensively on the PS3 and own it on the Switch as well.  Now after having completed the game entirely having gotten every achievement, I feel that is only proper I give it a review.

Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen is a philosophical masterpiece that explores the concepts of agency, will, cycles, meaning, and purpose in a thought provoking and intriguing way.  What is more is it does all of this while having combat that puts many modern RPGs to shame.  I don't think I've played another RPG that comes close to matching Dragon's Dogma in terms of gameplay.  If I have it was probably another Capcom game.

The narrative of Dragon's Dogma begins in a humble fishing village and will quickly takes you across the realm and into the heady depths of politics and intrigue.  However it is not in the narrative events, but the philosophical underpinnings surrounding them that the game finds its narrative value.  Most of the narrative serves to build up the world and the actors in it, so that the game can later use this to explore the philosophical  questions it seeks to explore.  Don't expect The Lord of The Rings though, this game was on a tight budget and it shows in places.  The narrative you are presented at face value is meager and lacking until you begin delving into the more heady philosophical questions the game first hints at, and then shoves blatantly into your face demanding an answer.  The Dark Arisen DLC expounds even further upon this by taking you to Bitter Black Isle, where you will uncover more about the world's lore that can help to paint a clearer picture.  Overall I would say this game's narrative is high quality in the areas that matter, but don't expect something that is easily digestible.  Hideaki Itsuno, the game's director, seems to be fan of a meta narratives and exploring deeper ideas rather than popcorn entertainment.  Skyrim this is not.

The gameplay of the game is built off of nine classes, each with their own unique abilities and limitations.  Though the spread of abilities and limitations was not equal.  With some classes being borderline useless in a number of fights, and others being able to build themselves such that they never have any issues anywhere.
 Balance issues aside though, the actual gameplay is very good.  Each class, with the exception of Warrior, gets six abilities.  Using Strider as an example, you will have three abilities for your daggers and three abilities for your bow.  In addition to having these six abilities though, you will also have light and heavy attacks available.  The game manages all of this through some very clever control mapping.  It is the skills themselves that are the real star of the show though, with nearly every skill in the game being interesting in some way.  Even if it is only for looking cool.  The game's balance issues due effect the skills to some degree though, and you will find that some skills never leave your loadout while you never seem to find a good use case for others.  One last tidbit for magic classes, you can hit L3/LS while casting a spell to manually aim.

Moving on to the world, Dragon's Dogma takes place in the world of Gransys.  And while it may be showing its age graphically now, I would contend it is still a beautiful and spectacular world.  More importantly though it is filled with unique and interesting creatures and a variety of quests.  I make no guarantees for the uniqueness of the quests, only the monsters.  Nor do I make a guarantee for the variety of the monsters, be prepared to hear your pawns shout "Wolves travel in packs Arisen!" many times.  You will find more than just wolves though with hordes of goblins, cyclops, chimera, and other mythological creatures.  You'll just find that some of them are far more common than others.  The ones you do find though will be a lot of fun to fight as Dragon's Dogma allows you to freely climb onto large enemies like cyclops and chimera, allowing you to directly attack their weak points.

Quests in Dragon's Dogma are fairly typical, you talk to an NPC and get told what to do or you go to a notice board and pick up a quest notice.  NPC given quests are the more interesting story given quests, while the more mundane slay 8 rabbits or 10 bats quests are relegated to the notice boards.  Quests given by NPCs however while largely optional, are with almost no exception, worth completing at least once.  The main Narrative thread of this game can be completed in a couple of hours if you're speedrunning it, so it is well worth spending the extra time on side quests as they come up.  This is especially true as certain points in the main quest will auto-fail certain uncompleted side quests if you don't do them first.  There is urgency to complete the side quests in this game, but there is also help.  

Early on you will make a character that will act as an AI controlled combatant to help you on your journey.  This character is called a Pawn, and your pawn may be hired by other players to help them on their journey just as you may hire other players pawns.  If your pawn is with another player when they complete a quest, they will obtain knowledge of that quest and when they return to your world they will be able to guide you through the quest according to the knowledge that they have.  Conversely you can hire a pawn that has knowledge of the quest you want to do.

The pawn system has many benefits beyond just the timely completion of quests though.  Pawns fight alongside you and by hiring additional pawns you can create a party of up to four ready to face whatever challenges await you.  Pawns aren't just hired mercenaries though.  They are a key part of the game's lore and learning more about them as you journey through the game will be important to understanding the world of Gransys.  And the gameplay design of Pawns reflects this, being a very deep and nuanced system.  Even to the point of its own detriment as it is all to easy to make a pawn that is detrimental rather than helpful.  Most of the pawns you find ingame whether auto-generated or human made will be awful.  With poor equipment, ability choices, inclinations, or a mix of all three.  You will want them though, Gransys is a very dangerous place to travel alone for the inexperienced.  Pawns bring many advantageous if you're judicial in your selection of them, and there are communities online where you can find other people's pawns to hire and get your pawn hired now.

Overall, I would say that Dragon's Dogma was ahead of its time in many ways and the industry still hasn't caught up to some of the elements of its design.  Pawns I'm talking about Pawns.  Why are this game and its sequel still the only games to use this feature in 2025? Get with the program RPG devs, developer made followers are a relic of a game that came out in 2011.  Player made followers is where it's at.  But yeah, the lore of the game is top notch, even if the initial presentation is lacking at first.  The game play knocks it out of the park even to this day, unlike a certain game that came out six months earlier.  And the Pawn system is a stroke of genius.  I give this game a 10/10 with highest honors.  May we see more games like it in the coming years, and fewer games that aren't worthy of comparison to this one.

In my opinion, one of the best games of all time. 

Few games have had as satisfying combat as Dragon's Dogma. Striders fluidly switch between raining arrows down on foes to climbing them and hacking at them directly. Sorcerers bring bombastic destruction to the field with falling meteors, tornadoes, and earthquakes. Fighters are unbreakable walls or invulnerable vortex of blades. Warriors bring earth shattering blows. Mystic Knights return damage in fantastically bursts of counter magic or lay enchantments to send volleys of magic at foes. Magick Archers carry a diverse set of skills to meet the situation including [i]lighting themselves on fire[/i]. Rangers either act as 50 cal snipers or literal tank cannons. There's so much to experience with each class and you can freely switch as you like to experiment.

The main world is vast, bright, and aesthetically pleasing though a bit barren. Enemies abound and there are clever little areas to visit throughout, but places you can really work through are few and far between. However, the expansion area, BItterblack Isle, is a dungeon crawl with loads of content packed densely. 

The story of the main game is quite a bit bare as you are told little aside from "kill the dragon" and then in the last 10% of the story the game just dumps lore on you. The expansion area has a story of its own that is better paced though told through notes found about and overheard conversations from the past.

And the fashion, oh the fashion. The game has one of the best character customization systems ever. You want to play as a 7ft tall Amazoness? Go ahead. How about a short, stout beared elf? That works too. How about a little old woman swinging a massive slab of steel? Swing away, granny. Adding on to this, levels are king in this game. Once you start leveling up, you can choose whatever armor you want with little repercussions meaning you can make your character look however you want.

And then there's the innovative Pawn System. In addition to creating your own character, you can create a sidekick and train them to suit your preferences. However, manipulating their AI to behave as you prefer is more than a bit obtuse though. Once made, you can then send them out into the world to help other players and bring other player's pawns into your own world to aid you. Most of the time, they'll be decent supports and meat shields, but in rare moments you'll see absolute brilliance that'll make see the potential characters like these have.

This game originally came out on the PS3/Xbox360 less than a year after after Skyrim and Dark Souls and was completely overshadowed by them. I fully believe if the game had been given a AAA-level budget, it could have been as massively impactful as both of those juggernauts on the gaming industry. As is, it is still a brilliant game and one I keep finding myself coming back to time and again cause it really is an ageless classic, even if it's just the 'hidden gem' that everyone seems to know about.

Dragon's Dogma is theoretically cool but practically boring.

Whether you stab the eye of a cyclops to send it reeling or burn the wings of a gryphon to bring it crashing to the ground, you're still going to spend the next five minutes chipping at their health bar. 

The game is hamstrung by three major issues: AI, stat scaling, and instant-use consumables.  In Dragon's Dogma, you fight alongside three AI controlled pawns - one of your own design and up to two rented from other players.  In addition to their skills and equipment, you can customize your pawn's combat priorities.  A pawn with the "mitigator" inclination will target weak foes, a "challenger" will chase ranged enemies, and so on. 

Despite this, pawns are idiotic.  My sorcerer pawn began to charge a long-casting meteor spell in striking range of a Living Armor, died, got revived, only to start charging again. The Living Armor is immune to physical damage beyond a certain point, so I was relying on my pawn to dispatch it once it reached low health.  

Furthermore, the game is balanced around a party of four - forgo or underequip pawns, and fights drag on and on.  And, because you're just one of four, most damage is dealt and taken between AI controlled enemies and AI controlled pawns.  You're a minority contributor.  That is to say, the game plays itself more than you play it.  

Enemy AI is also lackluster.  Most enemies won't be able to hit you if you move away from them. 
Here's a video where I stroll around about a dozen enemies in an end game zone for 30 seconds without getting hit.  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Fc6DGokQ-E

Pawns, however, lack the common sense to avoid attacks.  Do you see the problem here?  

Dragon Dogma's second major issue is the scaling of enemy health and armor. Armor is subtractive - that is, without appropriate gear, you will hit for 0 damage.   Going from 700 strength to 900 strength against an enemy with 500 armor will double the damage you inflict.   This system needlessly lengthens fights and gates parts of the game behind gear.

A quintessential example of these problems is the late game fight with [spoiler] Death. [/spoiler]  This enemy's offense is limited to two telegraphed melee-range attacks, both of which can be avoided by confidently walking in the other direction.  Of course, pawns don't dodge.  This enemy also has vast amounts of health and armor.  Because pawns succumb instantly, this enemy is unconfrontable until you can equip yourself with sufficiently strong gear.  Once you are capable of inflicting noticeable damage solo, the fight becomes an slowly-told joke.  

Finally, the infinitely-purchasable, instant-use consumables ruin all suspense.  In the midst of having my head bitten off by an Gorecyclops, I can pause, grab a Lordy Tonic from my pawn, and max my health. At best, combat becomes a war of attrition between the Cursed Dragon's eight health bars and my 20 Harspud Sauces.   At worst, fights are a just a tedious drag.  There's no tension and, once money becomes plentiful, no need for skillful play.

It's a shame, because the game has some really high points, especially when encountering a boss for the first time.  Classes and skills are varied and the spell effects are the best I've seen in any game.  But at the end of the day, whether you fight with a gigantic sword or by conjuring a maelstrom, most of the game is spent picking away at unthreatening beasts with oversized health bars, sipping potions, and reviving meatshield pawns.

The combat system is far ahead of its time. The game is huge and forgiving, while still being challenging. You might typically beat the main story by level 50, but the level system goes to 200, allowing you to literally become a God. I feel this game really shines in the Dark Souls-esque secondary story-line at the Bitter Black Isle. One of my top 3 RPG's of all time. If only there was a second.

It's the most kitchen sink and generic as possible game imaginable in presentation. Every single monster or enemy you fight is taken near straight from Dungeons and Dragons monster books.

And you know what? It's excellent. There's no nonsensical ambiguity, there's no elements that don't flow or work well. Everything belongs in the world and makes sense, because they focused on doing everything well rather than trying to be unique or special. This idea of surface level blandness is a facade to cover the depth of consideration and effort that went into the game in nearly every imaginable way. Whether it's the monsters, the aesthetics, or the gameplay itself.

There are precious few other games where your character's height and weight actually affects how you interact with the game world or how you fight specific enemies. There are precious few that have the ability to have your mage create gigantic ice pillars that you can then use as stepping stones to rapidly scale a cyclops or some other kind of wild shenanigans. 

For 30$ this game is a steal. It's Skyrim without Todd Howard lies.

Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen IS my favorite game, I loved it when it first came out in 2012, when I got multiple copies for various platforms, and even now! On PS4 I got to level 200 and I had only just got to the end of bitterblack isle, the DLC for the game. So I'm now reviewing my favorite game for the first time after eight YEARS of playing and enjoying. 

Short version: If you like big battles, great combat, lots of enemies, a story you have to make the connections to understand, some funny moments via the pawns being pawns, places to explore, cool weapons and armor. Then I think you'll like this game.

LONG DRAWN OUT VERSION CAUSE I'M GONNA PUT MY THOUGHTS ALL OUT THERE BUCKO:

Things I love, the big monster battles, and enemy variation. You can climb a cyclops and stab it in the eye! Climb a Drake's tail while it hovers, breathing fire on your pawns, just to deal massive damage while it's trying to shake you off. Grab a harpy's feet in order to go for a medieval esc. flight for a bit till your ride just decides to crash and burn! The combat is where the game is strong, mix and match vocations, move sets, weapons in order to get what kind of combat experience you enjoy most! It's so much fun to fight stuff! There's a lot of variation in combat, what to do, aanndd variant in enemies, There is a LOT of monsters and pretty much every monster has some sort of variation depending on where, and when you're at in the game. Some only appear end game, in caves, on Bitter Black isle. Each different kind comes with new tactics, new resistances, move sets and even design. 

Story. A lot of people I've talked to say "there isn't a story" and on the surface level things just seem like "kill the big bad dragon and get your heart back". So yeah there isn't much of a story if you just look at a surface level but the thing is, this game doesn't tell you that much of the lore or even what you're really doing. Most of the story comes to you gradually and is made by your own inferences and connections to what's going on. Once you make your own inferences after gradually realizing things, then the game becomes much more...existentialistic. However, to fully get certain concepts...a new game plus is required as new scenes and aspects of the story open up. Which is an advantage and disadvantage as if you didn't think there was much story there to begin with, then why play the game AGAIN? 

Since you get Pawns from other players. A Pawns skill, mannerisms, even general tactics depend entirely on someone else's main pawn. Some will throw you up into the air so you can get some more swings at a big monster, some will catch you if you fall from, then there's SOME who will stop and gather every little thing...even when in battle. I also find some of the things they say or mention to be rather funny and it gets a chuckle out of me. It's also fun to go into the rift and see some people's loving creations. 

A medium world with lots to do and explore. Just as it says, there are plenty of places to explore and even some areas which you question "why is there a chest here?". If you're the type of person to explore EVERY nook and cranny multiple times "just to be sure you didn't miss anything" there are PLENTY of places to do that with. 

Characters. Most main characters, such as Gregori, are well written and well voice acted. Little story things that surprised me even after playing a lot of the game. Such as "Oh I didn't know that person could be saved" and then hearing a small change in dialogue afterwards. and a few different ways to do quests that you won't know till you just decide to do something different. 

Customize your Arisen and Pawn with pre selected features, height, weight, a few sliders, different colored eyes and more to be either a thing of beauty or a bit of a "why did I make this" creation. 

and now for small things that I'm not fond of but don't ruin the game for me. 

A lot of back and forth. A word of caution to anyone who may be reading the reviews about this game's story. Dragon's Dogma has a fantastically deep story about the cycle of existence that is about as easy to figure out at solving a Rubik's Cube. There are no NPCs or narrators that sit you on their knee and tell you the story while you close your eyes and listen. The story of Dragon's Dogma is told through many hours of seemingly pointless side quests. If you skip the side quests you will miss out on pieces of a wonderful story. The world does indeed feel a bit empty, but that also is part of the story of Dragon's Dogma. The NPCs seem hollow, sure, but again that is part of the game's story. These oddities that you don't expect in an RPG are not design flaws or small things overlooked by the game's creators. This game is like a book with a slow start and a fantastic ending; with a beautifully conceptual story that you won't get the full gist of until the last boss of the post-game content.

I find the combat in Dragon's Dogma to be extremely impressive. Sure the game is fun if you play as a Strider and put on some daggers, climb the enemies, and go ham, but the fact that the game's combat mechanics work with a plethora of classes that all play differently is not easy to find in open world RPGs lately. You can play effectively as a mage, supporting your hired pawns through curatives and debilitations, or you can ditch your pawns entirely and play as an assassin who gets a massive stat boost from venturing forth alone. I've even played through the game with just a shield equipped and "perfect blocking" or riposting every enemy's attack. The depth of a game's mechanics and amount of time I'm able to sink into the game in an effort to learn them all is one thing that attracts me to RPG style games, and in that regard, Dragon's Dogma did not disappoint.

To those who feel that enemies have too much health, one of the game's mechanics is that enemies have a defense stat that your offense stat has to break through in order for you to deal more than 1 damage to them. If an enemy is taking you too long to defeat, you either have to get creative with items that do set damage like explosives, or try enhancing or replacing your weapons or leveling up a bit more. When you come back later, those same enemies that took 500 hits to kill will only take 3 or 4 hits. Most enemies also have specific weak points which will award them more damage. Bandits for example take extra damage if you hit them in the head. Figuring out the weakness of each enemy is an engaging part of Dragon's Dogma's combat, and once you master the combat system, you will find yourself able to deal with enemies that used to slaughter you.

I cannot help but recommend Dragon's Dogma, but I caution buying the game against anyone who is impatient or looking for an action game. Dragon's Dogma has a decently well hidden story that in my opinion is worth finding, but the journey does require a time sink, less it won't be enjoyable.

Unbelievably beautiful game.   The environments and backgrounds look like oil painting landscapes half the time, yet it's all playable.  If you're at the top of a mountain, and see some interesting  terrain feature, it's often something you can eventually reach  and climb around (There are of course, places that are out of bounds or "off the map", like any game).    

The game is also one of the most immersive games I've ever played.  Creeping through the night with torches is spookily atmospheric... and then quickly terrifying when enemies literally come charging out of the edge of the torchlight at you.  Dungeons are literally claustrophobic.   View distance is crazy, without bogging down the game.  I once stood and watched a chimera the size of a house rampaging through a section of woods from halfway across a valley (it was apparently fighting some lizardmen... I found that out, because I decided to go kill the chimera.  That... didn't...  work out very well at all.  Yeah, that sucked).  

Speaking of chimera's the size of houses, the game has boss monsters so big you jump onto them and climb around all over them, attacking and chopping at body parts and armor as you go,  For a few, this is basically an essential strategy.  On the chimera, you can attack and kill the snake headed tail, or the goat growing out of it's back and eventually kill those body parts (which means they stop shooting their attacks too by the way).

There's a very complex and detailed character skill/class system.   Your character can even switch from one class to another, gaining a very customized skill set and stats.  Your characters stats increase certain amounts based on the class you play as for each level, so you could play as a warrior for a certain number of levels, and then switch to a mage class.   You'll end up being a mage with lower magick related stats, but you'll have a lot more health and you'll generally be tougher then if you'd only been a mage for all those levels.  There are entire character build strategies based around started as one class, switching to a 2nd, and then a 3rd so you end up with certain skills and general stat ranges.  As you progress through one class, you grab certain skills that really really really benefit other classes you switch to later on.  Your "class" is also effectively the armor and gear you decide to wear at any given time, but you need to belong to certain classes to even use some types of gear at all.   So once you have stuff unlocked, you can switch back temporarily if you want.  So if you had been a warrior, and switched to a mage, you can literally still put on armor and use warrior weapons.  It will just make your magic casting suck terribly while you do that.  Over all the system is crazy flexible.

You not only have direct control over your player, but another NPC called a "pawn" (they're soulless magical creatures from some other magical dimension that just happen to look human when they're in ours).  You start with one "Pawn" who follows you throughout the game.  You have total control over the appearance, class, and skills of your pawn, and they follow ALL orders you give them without fail.    Your pawn's build can be used to strengthen or offset your own character:  If you're a warrior for example, you can make your pawn a magic caster or healer, to provide support, or an archer for DPS, or even another warrior that stands shoulder to shoulder with you.  Entirely up to you.  

The game also has another mechanism that allows you to bring in a 3rd and 4th NPC.   The extra two NPC's were actually other players main "pawns".  There was a server synchronization system that allowed you to upload your own main pawn, and then they could be browsed and downloaded by other players.   You could add up to  two pawns that were made by other players.   The 3rd and 4th pawns followed orders, but you had far less control over them.   They were "frozen" and couldn't be changed.   They came with whatever skills and behavior presets they were uploaded with.   So you could get a healer with no healing skills, if you weren't careful.  Archers with no bow equipped, etc.   A warrior with a shield, but no skills to use the shield effectively (shield bash, etc).   Some people uploaded some truly obnoxious broken non-sensical builds.   Some builds were really effective, and you could tell from the appearance and equipment they had that someone had spent a ton of time customizing them.  

These other NPC pawns also couldn't level up, at all.   They just stayed frozen exactly as you downloaded them.   So eventually, as your character and main pawn progressed through the game, you "outgrew" the other backup pawns, and they had to be replaced with higher level ones. 

I'm not 100% sure the upload/download system for the 3rd and 4th NPC is still working.  It required connecting to a server run by the game company to get a list of pawns uploaded by other players, and I think the server was shut down.

Even then, the game is playable with just your character and the main pawn (the game scales based on how many or how few NPCS you have, so adding the 3rd and 4th npc pawns actually made things harder).  The main advantage of using the downloaded pawns is they sometimes came with super high level weapons and gear, and rare skills (and no, you couldn't take their gear off of them, it went poof if you did).  Sometimes, other people's pawns were just a good snapshot for a "build", and they just worked super well.   Sometimes, they were just a convenient way to get some skills you didn't want to have on your main character or main pawn.
