Yet another "Played it back in the day" review, but it's really important to emphasize that. I have ample experience with this game. I'm not just posting a blind review just for a free thumbs-up.

So going into Dragon's Dogma, you've gotta keep one thing in mind: It was a console exclusive made before The Witcher 3, and shortly after Dark Souls and Skyrim. To compare it to the formermost is an unfair benchmark, because TW3 obviously came out years later and had time to take advantage of feedback for TW2 and, yes, Dragon's Dogma. To compare it to Dark Souls is to try to apples-and-oranges the gameplay comparison, as Dark Souls features a large diversity of individual weapons with nuances compared to Dragon's Dogma relatively same-y weapons coupled with unique RPG skills. And the Elder Scrolls, as a series, has a completely different exploratory feel to this game, but unlike Skyrim, Dragon's Dogma doesn't feel like it needs to lead you around by the hand to everything.

Now, what do you get when you play DD? The pros:

- Overall, it is an action-filled, open-world romp with 9 classes that feel completely different (hell, even ignoring the 3 'advanced' classes, you have 6 totally unique playstyles).

-A novel approach to partybuilding emphasizes gameplay first. No longer do you need to think "oh, man, should I take the guy who was complaining about his ex-wife, or the girl who was hitting on me?" Companions (Pawns in-game) are literally mindless automatons, and the game unabashedly accepts the fact. And because the game is more focused on the sheer spectacle of climbing all over monsters and hacking and slashing them as they try to buck you off (minus terrible QTEs or gauges that you have to manage), coupled with the encouragement (read: necessity) to change pawns on a regular basis as hirees don't level up, means that your party is as fluid as your playstyle can be.

-While we're at it -- look, I don't know many games that make it possible to go fluidly from relentlessly bashing monsters in the face with a sword, with no regard for your safety, one moment, re-classing, then performing screen-shaking active blocks with your elementally-charged shield, do you? Okay, sure, Skyrim, but Skyrim doesn't have the fact that in order to best level up, you NEED to vary between classes, both to manage stat growths (which differ based on what class you were when you leveled up) and to unlock passive skills which can be applied at any time to any class.

-The world may not be the biggest one ever concocted, but it feels alive. Feelin' froggy? Wander off the road and you'll find wild beasts (often of mythical origins) waiting to tear your party apart. Or, travel the roads at night and run into bandits. The fast-travel system is also intentionally gimped in the early parts of the game, and for once I actually felt like this was a good thing -- unlike The Witcher 3, where you can just gallop down a road for literally minutes seeing nothing along the way, in DD you see a cave off in the distance and decide to go explore it. Or you actually take a wrong turn, clear out an area, then realize you're going the wrong way. I know it sounds frustrating, but it's actually FUN. You actually feel like you're in a REAL WORLD.

-The story may be a bit bland, but it's got its share of political drama, tragedy, and revenge. Essentially, as I detailed above, you shouldn't really come into this game expecting to be blown away, but there are enough little tweaks to a rote formula to make it enjoyable.

-The magic is great enough to earn its own damned bulletpoint. Playing a Sorcerer in this game feels downright amazing. Spells rip the screen apart, from the lowly fireball to a massive sky-splitting meteor shower. And with the Pawn system, you really have to actually treat mages (whether it's you or pawned [heh] off to an NPC) like glass cannons, making them feel like true magical artillery.

Cons? Well:

-It's a game from 2012 (2011? Something like that), and it shows. Graphics, even uncompressed, are muddy, and you can either go with the dull coloration and odd tints of vanilla or use an injector like SweetFX and realize that the only way to fix certain things is to crush the blacks into a pulp. Unfortunate, that.

-Audio design really is nothing to write home about. The music is generic fantasy fare, but if you know anything about DD, you know that its dialogue is almost a running joke. Pawns will NOT SHUT UP. They say the SAME THING over and over. Did you know that wolves hunt in packs? Oh, you remember your pawn telling you that the last time you fought them about 200 feet up the road? Well, they'll remind you. Fortunately, this banter can be turned off with an in-game option, but... If you haven't played before, I recommend leaving it on for just a little bit, to understand what the old crowd of DD players dealt with.

-While I haven't experienced any issues whatsoever myself, running this game at 1080p on an external monitor from my laptop (with borderless fullscreen forced using a third-party software), bear in mind that a lot of people have apparently had issues with the game, tech-wise. Look up to see if people had issues with hardware close to yours before committing.

-In the endgame, after you've unlocked every vocation's skill, I'll be the first to admit that a lot of the magic of progression is gone. But... that's just it, in this it is NO DIFFERENT from any other RPG. I'm not sure why so many of the negative reviews imply that this is an issue of some sort. Nonetheless, with the many different playstyles available, you can easily just hotswap as you go, playing however you feel like at a certain moment.

-One savegame only. I remember reading the justification for this somewhere, but anyways, the game is basically oriented around having one character, and focusing in on the inevitable New Game+. Some people don't mind, others do. I leave this up to you. External backup programs are already floating around, allowing you to swap files, so check them out if this is a major breaking point.

Final Verdict:

It's not a modern AAA title. It's a 5-year-old AA title. Does this mean it's bad? Hell no. Dragon's Dogma was a cult hit for a reason. While I won't be so cocky as to imply it is so, I wouldn't be surprised if CDPR took a lot of notes from it as they created The Witcher 3. In a world of simplified ARPGs, Dragon's Dogma just took the idea of gameplay-first and ran with it. No, it probably won't make you cry or tug at your heartstrings, it won't even be particularly interesting, but if you look at it as a game, you will realize that it is fantastic at what it does.

Plus you can climb onto monsters and punch them until they die.

9/10 would punch a griffin to death again.

EDIT: This review was modified to get rid of my praise for The Witcher 3, because I thought that there was nearly-universal acclaim. To clarify, I had called it a 'modern masterpiece' because that sounded like the kind flower crap you put in reviews. Now, my profile said I've played it 50 minutes, this is untrue (a lot of time playing was spent offline), but I haven't beaten the game. I am not some massive TW3 fanboy. I just thought it was an okay, not-worth-60-bucks-but-still-okay, open-world RPG.

That said, if you didn't at least enjoy TW3, don't get Dragon's Dogma, because it feels very much so like DD is a less-detailed early version of TW3, with VERY similar world mechanics. The difference is that DD adds a layer of complexity through its class/vocation system that makes it more of an RPG, gameplay-wise, than TW3 was (obviously, the sidequests are much simpler in DD, and the main narrative is laughably bad compared to TW3 up until the last few hours of the main storyline).

This game is wonderful. I’m old enough now to know that tastes change, experiences change us,sometimes we lose ourselves and sometimes we regain more than we expected, and that we aren’t the same person we were long before our last breath. But if I were ever to say a game was my favorite, Dragon’s Dogma would be it. 

This game is an RPG and a sandbox world. You create your character--the hero of the journey--but you also create  a second character, who is your Pawn, someone to help and guide you through the story that lays ahead. You and your Pawn can be joined by two other Pawns, who are creations of actual people. This is a fantastic mechanic, as you can “rent” out your Pawn to other people, who will not only come back with a reward from an appreciative player, but also with knowledge of foes and quests that the other player exposed to them. Your Pawn, and other pawns, are constantly talking to you (unless you ask them not to) and guiding you through this world. It’s amazing, it’s funny, it’s annoying. 

The world itself is fantastic. The story is engaging. My first few playthroughs I couldn’t get into the game. It felt alien and weird. The game doesn’t hand things to you, so I found myself wandering around irritated that I didn’t know what I was supposed to be doing or what was going on. I’m an Arisen? What the hell is that? There’s a dragon waiting to kill me, why don’t I go straight to it and fight it, why am I stuck in this place? Then, as I was walking the streets to somewhere, I heard an NPC talk. NPC’s talk all the time, making comments to you or to another NPC. And while it wasn’t obvious they were talking about you or the game you were playing, the situation you found yourself in, they WERE. And it clicked. The game was about how you face your life, no matter what is thrown at you. The NPC’s came alive, I wanted to talk to them to see how they were handling this terrifying ordeal. Some were afraid, some wanted to check out, some wanted to fight, and some just didn’t see a change in their lives since they aren’t the ones who fight dragons. I found quests which reflected these interactions, and I discovered all the quests reflect them, and even the last battle itself. When faced with a horrible, impossible choice--who am I? What kind of person am I? What will I do? Will I take the easy path and lose that which are close to me? Or will I take a risk and not only win myself my life back--but also change the lives of others around me for the better? The game is very philosophical and I love it. 

The combat itself is good. You have classes you can level up (and change whenever you want), and each class has special skills. You can use those skills, you can also grab and hold enemies so your pawns can beat up on them. You can also carry an enemy and throw them off a cliff if you want. There are giant monsters you have to face, and you can use the grab mechanic to CLIMB UP THEM. I always enjoy climbing a cyclop’s back and wailing on their head. 

Also, there is a love mechanic, the game doesn’t tell you, so you’ll want to do some research before your girlfriend is a 12 year old girl or a big, sweaty, hairy blacksmith, because you can’t change that, it happens when it happens, you’re stuck with that. So….yeah.

I bought Dragon's Dogma during Summer sale for 12$, I heard it was good game but didn't really expect much, thought it was just "another RPG" but it turned out to be one of the best RPGs I've ever played.

It's hard to compare DD:DA with other RPGs, it is a mixture of all the best things you've played from other video games: the non-linear sandbox structure from Elder Scrolls games, the giant boss mechanic from Shadow of The Colossus, the badass combat mechanic from Devil May Cry, the challenges that require survival and management skill from Dark Souls and classic RPGs. Because of this, DD:DA is one of the most underrated, fun and well-designed RPG ever made.

Pros:
- Perfect combat system (if not almost). As mentioned, the combat has elements from action games such as Devil May Cry, Dark Souls,... every monsters have weak spots that you must learn while fighting them, and there are epic giant boss fights similar to fighting a colossus in SoTC. What makes combat so satisfying are the badass animations and badass skills, combine with the sounds and gore effects, you can feel every strikes you inflict on the enemy. You can also change class easily and enjoy your own playstyle without having to worry about optimal build. 

- Pawn system: you must create a custom companion for yourself, its appearance, personality, class will be your invention. As you progress, this pawn will learn from you and become more aware with the world such as how to find a weak spot on monster, how to do a certain quest easier,... The online feature of this game is that you can let people hire this pawn of you to help them as you can hire people's pawns to help you. It's a complex system but also very rewarding and gives meaning to your progress. To keep it short: you are giving life to an AI.

- Rich character customization system: you can pretty much create anyone, just google "Dragon Dogma Character Creation" and you will see what I'm talking about. Also, armors and clothing are excellent designed and varied to serve your fashion obsession, there are also well animated cloaks to increase your badass-ness.

- Great and memorable music.

- The big bad dragon is twice the size and twice the challenge of Alduin from Skyrim, he also says things that will leave you pondering, I kid you not. 


Neutral:
- Lot of people say this game has no story at all, I disagree. Story in this game is minimal and somewhat predictable, but it's there and it has very interesting lore that you must figure out by yourself. And if it helps, I'm the kind who prefer story over gameplay and I think this game does great enough for its minimal storytelling.


Cons:
- Notice board quests aka MMO fetch quest: while they can be fun to do in early game and makes the game feel alive, there are just too many of them and most of it are more trouble than it's worth (e.g: take this guy to that place that's at the end of your unexplored map, kill 50 of this thing that you just killed a bunch of them an hour ago,...). So It's only recommended to do these quests if you are interest in the reward or looking to farm exp. 

- Due to the vague, non-linear structure of the game, the chance for you to miss something is high and the consequence can be severe. So it's recommended to check out the missable quests guide if you don't want to missing out.

- Some voice actors can be laughable bad.

- The above are just minor things, however, there is one thing I really dislike about this game: the terrible late game grinding, especially Dark Arisen's content. If you want those fancy late game loot, you must either spend another 20 hours to grind for it or using trick to still grind for it but in an hour or two, because these rare loot have a dropping chance of 2%, seriously. It get worse with the DLC where the game will prevent you from using the farming method from base game, and while the loot have better chances to drop in DLC, you will most likely get the same loot 3-4 times while wasting a bunch of currency that's mostly coming from people who hired your pawn, so you will definitely be screwed if no one hires your pawn.


In the end, over 100 hours of fun for a 12$ game is more than I could have asked for. I can say that I've never been addicted to a non-linear open world RPG like this since Skyrim, and it means this is the kind of game that will stuck in my hard drive for a very long time.

To be blunt: one of my favourite games ever.
Dragons Dogma: Dark Arisen is one of the few games i could never grow tired off.

[h1] Vocations [/h1]
When you first start playing you will have a choice between three Vocations (Classes), Fighter, Strider and Mage.
However these are not all Vocations, there are more you can unlock while playing, there are 9 Classes in total.
You can level them how you want as you can switch how often you want, there are two types of level, Character Level and Vocation Level, Character Level goes up to 200 and is shared across your entire save, Vocation level on the other hand goes up to 10 and every Vocation level unlocks either a new Skill for purchase at the Vocation NPC or a new Passive, Passives are shared between all classes, resulting in the player being able to build their chosen Vocation how they want and giving the player more reason to level other Vocations, playing an Assassin and you feel like your damage is a bit low? level a warrior a bit and grab the damage boost Passives.
However when switching to one of these Vocations you will notice one major thing, Stats, every single time you level up with your Character Level you gain a stat boost according to your Class which is permanent, meaning mixing up different types of classes will result in you being rather weak.
To make it easier: you played 100 levels as Sorcerer but suddenly you want to play Warrior, the issue is your damage will be extremely low compared to someone who was playing physical classes all the time mainly because all your stats will be Magic Focused.
However there are the Hybrid Classes which profit from mixed stats such as the Magick Knight who profits from Physical Damage as well as Magic Damage.

[h1] Pawns [/h1]
The game has a unique feature known as "Pawns", these Pawns are basically companions, however these pawn come with different sets of skills, equipment etc. early on in the game you will be prompted to create a "Main Pawn" a Main Pawn is pretty much part of you, meaning you cant really get rid of your Main Pawn. You can equip your Main Pawn with Skills, Armor etc. pretty much everything your Main Character has, you can even change the Vocation of your Pawn, your pawns Vocations all work the same as your Main Characters, however your Pawn does not have access to Hybrid Classes like you do.

When playing on the Online mode your pawn gets uploaded/updated in the Rift every single time you rest in an Inn.
The Rift is a hub filled with Pawns, when offline its filled with random generated pawns and when online from other players, meaning once your Pawn is uploaded other players will be able to "rent" your pawn, meaning they have your pawn as a party member, you can do the same, you can have up to 3 Pawns in your Group, you can rent them by spending "Rift Crystals" which is a currency mainly used for renting pawns, you earn these when someone rents your pawn and by just playing the game.

There is one major issue people seem to have with Pawns, talking.
Pawns talk ALOT in this game especially when in combat, i personally dont mind it but some people have an issue with that and i do understand why, hearing " 'TIS WEAK TO FIRE" or "WOLVES HUNT IN PACKS" for the 100th time can get on ones nerves.
For that you can turn off Pawn chatter in the options, though i personally advise against it mainly because Pawns often give information based on your current location or generally the lore and sometimes even their own opinion on the Story.

[h1] Combat [/h1]
The Combat in this game is as fluid as it can get, you have alot of freedom when in Combat, from literally grabbing your opponent and letting your Pawns club them to death to casting enormous spells, with absolutely devastating effects.
Wanna obliterate you Enemy? Why not summon a gigantic Tornado in their faces or summon a Meteor Shower.
When you are facing a bigger boss, you have the option to cling to them and actually climb them, once you are onto them you can attack them and in some cases use Skills.
Fighting a Big Cyclops? just climb towards his Eye and stab it.

Some people tend to compare this games Combat System with Dark Souls mainly because Enemies hit pretty hard in the beginning and your Attacks consume Stamina etc.
Others tend to compare it to Devil May Cry mainly cause you can combo your enemy to death and cause the Combat feels so fluid.
I personally say its neither of those or a hybrid at best.

What i personally love about this game the most is the fact that based on your Characters: Height, Weight and Muscle Mass you have different stats.
Meaning that if you have a small character, it results in you having less Power which results in you having less Carry Capacity but for that your Stamina Regeneration is higher.

[h1] Story [/h1]
The Story in this game is absolutely Amazing, when you first start it wont be very unique as it sounds like every other Fantasy RPG there is and once you progress a little you will be actually lost, as this game doesnt hold your hand like most RPGs do, no quest indicator or main story you can follow.
Do some random quests you find and at some point you will start to get a vague direction, which leads to a fully fledged storyline with an Ending which slightly changes when you go into New Game+ (Offline Mode) 

[h1] Stuff to do [/h1]
Due to this being Dark Arisen there is a unique Isle in the game called "The Bitterblack Isle" which is an entire island full of challenges and a rather Dark and Emotional Story once you manage to get through it.
Bitterblack Isle is meant as a huge Challenge, meaning if you run in there low level you will most likely die in the first room.
However if you manage to survive and get through some bosses you will be richly rewarded with a ton of Rift Crystals, High end gear and lots of Gold.
Note: When you complete Bitterblack Isle once it will change into some sort of Hardmode, making it even more of a challenge as there are new Enemies, Better Loot and a changed Final boss.

Other than BBI (Bitterblack Isle) you can simply do Board quests, which involve a Hunting Board (Hunt a specific Monster/Hunt a specific amount of Monsters), Escort Quests (Simply Escort an NPC to the said Location) and Collect Quests (Collect a specific Item)
All Boards have a limited amount of Quests, some with Awesome Rewards and some with bad Rewards, however completing certain Board Quests unlock unique new ones with better rewards etc.
There are multiple Boards and every Board has different types of quests they offer, example: the board in the Main Capital only offers Escort Quests.

There is always something to do in Dragons Dogma, from BBI to Boards to simply perfecting your Class and your Main Pawn.

[h1] Lastly [/h1]
I just randomly decided to write this review and it is nowhere near perfect, however i felt like i had to write this due to my massive respect for this game.

[h1] I personally rate this Game: 7/10 [/h1]
Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen has its ups and downs, if you can get past its issues then you are in for an amazing experience.
